1.
What is National Health
Workforce Accounts (NHWA)?
The purpose of the NHWA is to facilitate the standardization 
of a health workforce information system in order to improve 
data quality, as well as to support tracking HRH policy 
performance towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC). 
The NHWA is built up of core indicators and data characteristics that can be progressively measured in order: 
•	 generate reliable HRH information and evidence; 
•	 enable the planning, implementation and monitoring of 
workforce policies towards UHC; 
•	 improve the comparability of the health workforc

summary.text: Defines National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) as a system of core indicators and data characteristics designed to standardize health workforce information systems, improve data quality and comparability, and track human resources for health (HRH) policy performance towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC).

summary.text: Outlines the national, regional, and global relevance of engaging in NHWA, listing seven core benefits including understanding workforce equity and gaps, informing education scale-up and intersectoral dialogue across health, education, and finance ministries, guiding priority investments, and fostering cross-country data comparability.

3.
The 2030 Agenda gives recognition to UHC as key to achieving all 
other health targets. SDG 3c sets a target to “substantially increase 
health financing and the recruitment, development, training and 
retention of the health workforce in developing countries, especially 
in least developed countries and small island developing States”. 
The report of the High Level Commission for Health Employment and 
Economic Growth recommends strengthening evidence, accountability and action, that could be obtained through NHWA.
Rationale:
Policy frameworks,
mandate and context of NHWA

summary.text: Presents the global policy rationale and mandate for NHWA within the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (specifically SDG target 3.c on health financing and health workforce recruitment, training, and retention) and the recommendations of the High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth.

Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH) to accelerate progress 
towards UHC and the SDGs by ensuring equitable 
access to health workers within strengthened

summary.text: Describes the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH) and World Health Assembly resolution WHA69.19 (May 2016), which urges Member States to consolidate core HRH data for annual reporting to the Global Health Observatory and progressively implement NHWA.

summary.text: Introduces the major health workforce policy questions that NHWA helps answer, covering (1) workforce profile (availability, accessibility, acceptability, and competencies), (2) production and deployment trends, and (3) distribution and productivity gaps by occupation, equity, and skill mix.

summary.text: Continues the list of policy questions addressed by NHWA, covering (4) addressing gaps through resource allocation, retention, and public-private partnerships, (5) improving performance and productivity, (6) balancing domestic workforce production against exits from retirement, mortality, and migration, and (7) evaluating financial incentives for geographical equity in underserved areas.

blocks.title: Page 8
blocks.content:
+ 8 +
5.
Why a Labour Market
analysis approach?
The NHWA uses a Labour Market analysis framework. This 
framework provides a comprehensive picture of health 
labour market dynamics through the contribution of four 
groups of health workforce policies – production; inflows 
and outflows; distribution and inefficiencies; regulation of 
the private sector – and the interplay these have in ensuring 
equitable access to quality services.

summary.text: Explains why NHWA uses a health labour market analysis approach, capturing the interplay of four policy domains—workforce production, inflows and outflows, maldistribution and inefficiencies, and private-sector regulation—in achieving equitable access to quality health services.

How was the NHWA
handbook developed? 
6.
The NHWA indicators was developed through a stepwise 
process that included several phases of consultation  with  
experts from around the world, including deans of faculty, 
academics, teaching instructors, information systems 
experts, policy planners, and health professionals from both 
developed and developing countries. 
Experts of the Technical Advisory Group representing various 
institutions engaged in HRH data monitoring, collection and 
management, discussed and interpreted the results of a 
global consultation, among others, in a serie

summary.text: Summarizes the stepwise development of the NHWA handbook and indicators through global expert consultations and Technical Advisory Group workshops at WHO headquarters, selecting indicators based on relevance, availability, and national utilization aligned with the health labour market framework.

blocks.title: Page 11
blocks.content:

How is the NHWA
handbook structured?
Each of the 10 modules contains a set of indicators with 
declared policy relevance. These include both numeric and 
capability indicators that can provide information on regulation and other mechanisms related to the health workforce, 
and the status of the HRH monitoring and management 
system. 
7.

summary.text: Describes the structure of the NHWA handbook across 10 modules, each containing policy-relevant numeric and capability indicators covering health workforce regulation, management mechanisms, and HRH monitoring systems.

summary.text: Illustrates the 10 modules of the NHWA organized across three overarching domains—Education (Modules 2–4: workforce in education, regulation, and finances), Labour Force (Modules 1 and 5–7: active stock, labour market flows, employment conditions, and spending/remuneration), and Serving Population Health Needs (Modules 8–9: skill mix and performance/productivity)—supported by Module 10 on governance, information systems, and planning.
